job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in Eastfield with two mates, Callum and Raj, so the flat is loud and the fridge is a war zone. I do applications before lunch and then go for a long run, because I think better after. In the afternoon I teach myself a CAD package I didn't get on with at uni. I finished mechanical engineering seven months ago, top of the class, and my final project was a test rig for a wind turbine gearbox. I did two internships, one at a pump manufacturer, Garrow Pumps, and one on a factory maintenance team. I've applied everywhere I'd be happy and some places I wouldn't, and I've had no offer yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd shrug. I'd say fine, and tell my mates it's good news for anyone who works with machines. Online I'd say nothing, because I'm not the sort to post. At the pub I'd say the hype hurt hiring more than the tech helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same slow grind. There are some openings round here, a couple in manufacturing and a few in energy, but they want two years' experience for everything. I've had 80 applications and about six interviews. The rent for my share is 380 a month, and I've got maybe eight weeks of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, and I'd pick two firms and email the engineers directly, not the HR portal. I'd also take a temp job at the distribution centre, driving a forklift, which I'm qualified for. And I'd finish a small portfolio of my gearbox work, with photos and numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, a bit impatient. Like when you hold a spanner and the bolt won't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned emailing engineers directly. Why does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because engineers remember what it's like to be the new guy. HR is looking for keywords, but an engineer reads the first line and sees if you know what a bearing is. Callum got his job that way, and he's not even top of the class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a temp job at the distribution centre mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly, around 1,400 a month. And a reason to get out of bed. I wouldn't tell anyone back at uni, which is silly, since there's nothing wrong with it. But it feels like a step sideways.

say: I'd shrug and tell mates it's good news for anyone working with **machines**.
I'd say the hype hurt **hiring** more than the technology helped.
think: It's the same slow **grind**: openings exist, but they all want two years' experience.
I have maybe **eight weeks** of cushion with 380 a month in rent.
do: Email two firms' **engineers** directly instead of using the HR portal.
Take a **forklift temp job** at the distribution centre.
Finish a **portfolio** of my gearbox project with photos and numbers.
feel: **Flat** and impatient, like a bolt that won't turn.

steps.text: Email two firms' engineers directly with my gearbox portfolio
Apply for graduate roles in manufacturing and energy every day
Take a forklift temp job at the distribution centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like it's mostly an office story. A factory floor still needs someone to stand there and fix the pump when it screams. I'd tell mates to learn what the tools can do, but not to hand over the thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Design, simulation and reports are the thinking part of my job, and they're what juniors do first. If tools take that over, the junior desk goes, but a lot of maintenance and testing stays. That's the part where I got my hands dirty on the gearbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools to speed up my CAD work and my reports, and be able to say so in interviews. I'd target roles in testing, maintenance and commissioning, where you're on the shop floor. And I'd ask Garrow Pumps whether they'd take me on for a short contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, a bit nervous. Like a new tool in the shed. Good if you learn the new tool, risky if the new tool learns you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools. What would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try them on my CAD drawings and a stress analysis, then check by hand. I used one on my project report last term to tidy my language. It saved an evening, and it also got one number wrong, so I now check everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this change who you'd blame for a bad market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd blame firms for overhiring in boom years and over-firing in bad ones. The tools are just the latest excuse. Governments should smooth that out with graduate placement schemes, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

I'd rather be known for **hands-on** problem-solving than for typing.
do: Use the tools on **CAD drawings** and a stress analysis, then check by hand.
Target **testing, maintenance and commissioning** roles on the shop floor.
Ask **Garrow Pumps** about a short contract.

steps.text: Use AI on CAD drawings and a stress analysis, then check by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a short fuse. I'd say we need rules and a safety net now, and I'd say it plainly rather than getting heated. I'd tell mates to save every spare pound, and to keep a hands-on skill alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the thinking side of engineering is what goes first. The design office could be a tenth of its size. But a robot that can do a plumber's job isn't until about 2031, which gives me maybe three years to move into something physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd take the temp forklift job straight away and sign up for an electrician's course at the college, evenings. I'd go to the commissioning firms and say I'll work on site, whatever the pay. And I'd cut my spending down to bare rent and food, and move home if rent became too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty tense. Like waiting for the result of a scan: you don't know yet, but you can't think about anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said move home if rent got too much. Where is home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small town called Bexley, about two hours away. My mum and my stepdad have a box room. I'd hate it, but I'd do it, and I'd tell the lads honestly. They'd understand because Callum's already considered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost you to switch to a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand for the course and a few months at a lower wage. I'd say it's worth it if I get a job that's safe until 2031 and gives me skills to build on. A trade course is an insurance policy with a premium I can afford.

say: I'd say we need **safety net** now, said plainly rather than heatedly.
I'd tell mates to **save** and keep a hands-on skill alive.
think: The thinking side of engineering goes first, and the design office could shrink to a **tenth**.
I'd have about **three years** to move into something physical before robots catch up.
do: Take the **forklift job** straight away and start an evening electrician's course.
Tell commissioning firms I'll work **on site** at any pay.
Cut spending to rent and food, and be ready to move to **Bexley**.
feel: Pretty **tense**, like waiting for a scan result you can't stop thinking about.
S2.quote: A trade course is an insurance policy with a premium I can afford.
fieldNote: David's plan is an **insurance policy**: a trade course costing about two thousand.

He stays dry in tone, but the plan is **urgent**.

steps.text: Start an evening electrician's course at the college
Take the forklift temp job at the distribution centre straight away
Cut spending to bare rent and food
Move back to my mum's in Bexley if rent gets too much

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to do something with, which is all I'd ask. I'd tell mates to get a foot in now and stop waiting for the perfect offer. I'd say the government should offer retraining credits to anyone who loses a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see it as a decent window. If I land an engineering job this year, I'd get about four years in the field before the machines catch up on the thinking side. And I'd have time to be good at commissioning and testing, which is the physical end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first proper engineering job, even at 28,000, and get my chartered status started. I'd use AI tools for the paperwork and always check them. I'd put about 300 a month into savings, and I'd stay on the lookout for jobs on the physical, machine side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not thrilled, not scared. Like a long drive where you've got the satnav on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most likely way your plan goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first job doesn't come. Everything depends on getting in this year. If I'm still looking in 18 months, I'd be a graduate with a gap, and the five years start to look like a lot less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about working with AI tools at that stage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, as long as I'm the one signing off. It'd be like working with a sharp apprentice who sometimes makes things up. I'd use the help but never give the AI the keys.

I'd back **retraining credits** for anyone who loses work.
think: A job this year gives about **four years** in the field before machines catch up on thinking.
The plan fails if the **first job** doesn't come in the next year.

steps.text: Accept the first proper engineering job even at 28,000

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd call manageable. I'd tell mates to enjoy it, but not sleepwalk. I'd say governments should start practising now with small retraining schemes, so they're ready when it counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. A decade is a whole career's first third. I could get to senior engineer by then, and I'd have seen what the machines can and can't do. The first two years are the problem, since I'm not in work yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd land a job in the next six months, and move out of the shared room into a flat with my girlfriend, Hana, by 26. I'd use the tools every week and take a part-time master's in something like robotics maintenance. I'd also put some money into an index fund and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed. It's like seeing the weather forecast ten days out. You pack for it and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is Hana, and how does she fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's my girlfriend, a nurse, three years older. She'd be the stable income in a flat we'd share. I'd tell her honestly if I didn't have a job, and she'd say we'd manage, but I'd want to pay my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from your parents' generation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They stayed in one job for 30 years, and my stepdad got caught out when his firm closed. I'd keep my CV alive, stay curious about new tools and not trust one employer. It's a lot less secure, but it's honest.

I'd say small **retraining schemes** should start early.

The **first two years** are the problem, since I'm not in work yet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. That's when everything I've built so far turns out to be worth less before I've used it. What would help is retraining credits, an easy route into trade work, and firms being told to hire graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm good at looking calm. People think I'm relaxed, but I count my savings in weeks. I'd like to prove I'm worth hiring before somebody decides a machine is.

headlineQuote: People think I'm relaxed, but I count my savings in weeks.
portrait: David is a 23-year-old **mechanical engineering** graduate, top of his class, sharing a rented room in Eastfield with two friends.
He has had 80 applications and six interviews, with about **eight weeks** of cushion and 380 a month in rent.
He is a pragmatist in the centre who blames boom-and-bust **hiring** and wants retraining credits and graduate placements.
He tries AI tools once they're proven, checks the result by hand and moves toward **testing and commissioning**.
His girlfriend Hana, a nurse, and his mum's box room in **Bexley** are his safety net.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries him most, with his training worth less before he's used it.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **retraining credits**, an easy route into trade work and firms told to keep hiring graduates.
